name: Gareth Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Gareth. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm on a distribution crew out of the Millbrook depot, so mostly 11,000-volt lines on wooden poles running out to farms and villages. We sign on at seven, get the job sheet, load the truck and drive up the valley, and most days it's changing a rotten pole, swapping a cross-arm or restringing a span a tree took down. I like being up the pole on a clear morning with the whole valley under you. What wears me out is the call-outs at two in the morning in sideways rain.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How long have you been doing it, and what's home like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Six years now, counting the apprenticeship. I live with my girlfriend Leila in a rented flat over the hardware shop on Station Road, and she does home care visits, so between us we're never both home. Money's tight, honestly. I'm on the lower end of the pay band and we've got maybe two weeks of bills put by, so the storm overtime is what keeps us level.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, told you so. Half the lads at the depot have been winding each other up that a robot's coming for the poles, and I always said nobody's building a machine that can climb a rotten larch pole in a gale. I'd probably post something smug in the union group chat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it doesn't change much for me, because my problem was never AI. My problem is that rent on the flat went up again in March and the depot keeps talking about cutting standby rotas. If they cut the standby money, we're short by about four hundred a month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep doing what I do, keep my name on every storm list going. I'd push at the union branch meeting to fight any cut to the standby rota, because that's the real threat. And I'd try to stop us dipping into the overdraft every January.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of relief, but not much, because the same worries are still sitting there. I'm not lying awake about robots in that picture. I'm lying awake about the rent letter.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the overtime keeps you level. What happens in a calm winter with no storms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then we're in trouble by February. Last winter was mild and we put the car insurance on the credit card and we're still paying that off. Leila picked up extra Sunday visits to cover it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which bill goes unpaid first if the standby money goes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The credit card minimum gets paid, everything else gets juggled. We'd probably stop the car and I'd cadge lifts to the depot off Dev, who lives two streets over. That's the first thing, the car.

say: **Nobody's building** a robot that can climb a rotten pole in a gale, and I said so all along.
The real fight at the depot is **standby pay**, not some machine.
think: My worry was never AI; it's **rent** going up and our thin savings.
Losing the **standby rota** would leave us about four hundred a month short.
do: Put my name on **every storm list** so I don't miss any overtime.
Push the **union branch** to block any cut to the standby rota.
Try to keep us out of the **overdraft** every January.
feel: Some **relief** that robots aren't coming, but the **money worry** stays exactly where it was.
S0.quote: My problem was never AI. My problem is that rent on the flat went up again in March and the depot keeps talking about cutting standby rotas.
fieldNote: His **job** feels secure, but the **thin cushion** and overtime dependence keep him on edge.
He sees the **union** as his main tool and talks about it before anything else.
A **mild winter** already pushed the couple onto a credit card last year.

steps.text: Sign up for every storm call-out list at the Millbrook depot
Speak at the union branch meeting against cutting standby rotas
Pay down the credit card from the car insurance before January

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office that should worry, not us. The planners and the call centre, sure, but you can't answer a fault over the phone when the line's lying across the road. I'd say that at the depot and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it worries me more than I let on. Our job sheets already come off a system, and if a computer starts deciding which faults get a crew and which wait, they'll squeeze standby down to the bone. And the company is already flying drones along the lines to spot cracked insulators, which used to be a day of overtime walking the route for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put and keep my head down, because there's nothing else up the valley paying anything like this. I'd get the union to demand that any new scheduling system gets checked by people before it cuts rotas. I won't be learning the apps unless they make me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On edge, like the ground's shifting a bit under the van. Not the job itself, but all the bits around it that make the money add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you won't learn the apps unless they make you. What if the young lads pick it up and you don't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then they'll get the easy jobs with the tablet and I'll get the muddy ones, which suits me fine to be honest. I just don't want a screen telling me how long a pole change should take. I've seen poles that took four hours because the ground was solid rock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sandra in the control room, for sure. She's been there twenty years taking fault calls and she knows every farm by name. If a computer takes the calls, she's gone, and she's the one who sends us the right way when the map's wrong.

say: The **office jobs** should worry, because nobody answers a downed line over the phone.
Out on the poles, **hands-on crews** are still needed whatever software comes in.
think: A computer planning faults could **squeeze standby** and the overtime I rely on.
**Drone patrols** are already taking the line-walking days that used to pay extra.
do: Stay at the **Millbrook depot**, because nothing else nearby pays like it.
Push the union so any **scheduling system** gets checked before it cuts rotas.
Avoid the new apps unless the company **makes it compulsory**.
feel: **On edge**, as if the ground is shifting under the things that make the money **add up**.
S1.quote: The company is already flying drones along the lines to spot cracked insulators, which used to be a day of overtime walking the route for me.
fieldNote: He talks down the threat in public but privately sees his **overtime shrinking**.
With **few jobs nearby** and two weeks of savings, losing extras would hurt fast.
He worries about **Sandra in control**, which shows loyalty to colleagues over tech.
He prefers the muddy work to **learning tablets**, a firm choice for the familiar.

steps.text: Stay on the Millbrook crew rather than look for other work
Ask the union to demand checks on any new rota software
Cancel the gym and streaming to cover lost line-walking overtime

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be loud about it. I'd say the government needs to step in, tax these companies and look after people, because this is the bosses getting rid of all of us at once. I'd be at every union meeting and probably on a march.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means I've got about five years, maybe less. The thinking AI takes the planners and Sandra and whoever writes our job sheets in 2028, and then in 2031 a machine that climbs as well as I do turns up. I'm 27 and I don't know how to do anything else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending anything I don't need, straight away. I'd join every action the union runs and write to our MP about a guarantee for line crews. And I'd probably talk to Leila about moving back in with her mum to save the rent, which I'd hate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick, honestly. Like when the bucket truck lurched once on soft ground with me up in it. That drop in your stomach, but lasting for years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't know how to do anything else. Would you retrain?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd like to say yes. But retrain in what, if the machines are coming for everything by 2031? I'm not sitting in a classroom for two years to learn a job that's gone before I finish.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Leila that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my girlfriend Leila that we're not having kids until we know there's a wage. We'd talked about maybe in three years. That would be off.

say: The **government** must tax these firms and look after the people being pushed out.
I'd be at every **union meeting** and probably on a march.
think: I've got about **five years** before a robot that climbs like me arrives.
At 27 I don't know **any other trade**, and there's little work nearby.
do: Cut all **spending** I don't need from the first month.
Write to our **MP** demanding a guarantee for line crews.
Talk to Leila about **moving in** with her mum to save rent.
feel: **Sick**, like the bucket truck lurching on soft ground, but lasting for **years**.
S2.quote: I'm 27 and I don't know how to do anything else.
fieldNote: He sees **2031 robots** as the end of his job and has no backup skill.
He rejects **retraining** because he can't see a safe field to retrain into.
The news would **delay children**, which he raised himself, unprompted.
His anger points at **bosses and government**, in line with his politics.

steps.text: Cut takeaways, the car and anything not essential from the first month
March and strike with the union if crews face cuts
Write to the local MP demanding a jobs guarantee for line crews
Move in with Leila's mum to stop paying rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really, but with more time to organise. I'd be saying the union has to get a deal in writing now, while the company still needs us. Five years is enough to fight properly if people wake up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it buys me eight years until the robots climb, and that's more breathing room than the fast one. The planning side goes first in 2031, so the job sheets and the scheduling turn to software, but somebody still has to go up the pole until 2034. I'd be 35. That's young to be finished but not hopeless.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get on the union's negotiating committee, which I've never bothered with before. I'd try to put away fifty a week, even if it's hard. And I'd keep my head down at work so I'm not first on any list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but more like a heavy rain coming than a storm already here. I can see it from far off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Fifty a week is a lot when you've got two weeks saved. Where does it come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: From the pub on Fridays and the car, mostly. Leila's said for ages we should share her car, so I'd give in on that. It's not much but it's something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at a different job before 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I'd rather stay and fight for a good exit deal than jump to something I'd be rubbish at. If they want us gone, they can pay us properly.

say: The union must get a **written deal** now, while the company still needs crews.
Five years is **enough time** to fight properly if people wake up.
think: I'd have until **2034** before robots climb, which is more breathing room.
At **35** I'd be young to be finished, but it isn't hopeless.
do: Join the union's **negotiating committee** for the first time.
Put away **fifty a week** by dropping the pub and sharing Leila's car.
Keep my head down so I'm **not first** on any cut list.
feel: **Worried**, like heavy rain coming that I can see from **far off**.
S3.quote: I'd rather stay and fight for a good exit deal than jump to something I'd be rubbish at.
fieldNote: More time turns him from **protest** to **negotiation**, a real shift.
He still won't consider **changing jobs**, only a better exit.
Saving **fifty a week** is a stretch given two weeks of savings.

steps.text: Join the union's negotiating committee at the depot
Save fifty a week by sharing Leila's car and skipping the pub
Keep working the same crew and avoid standing out

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got ten years, so let's use them to get proper protections in law. Public ownership of the grid, a jobs guarantee, whatever it takes. I'd be saying that in the pub and online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years sounds like a lot, but I know me, I'll waste half of it hoping it won't happen. The robots come around 2039 and I'd be 40. That's the worst age to start over, with no degree and a body that's done twenty years of climbing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working, keep saving what I can, and keep pushing the union. Maybe in a few years I'd look at a training course for substation work, because I heard that might hold on longer. But I wouldn't do anything this year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unsettled. Less scared than the two-year one, but it nags at me. It's the kind of thing that sits at the back of your head on a long drive up the valley.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd waste half of it hoping. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because that's what I did with the apprenticeship exams. I put it off until the last month. I'm just not someone who jumps early, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Leila do differently with ten years' warning?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably still try for a kid, maybe in four years. But we'd want a council flat or something cheaper, not another private rent that goes up every March.

say: Ten years is time to get **protections in law**, like public ownership and a jobs guarantee.
I'd make that **case** at the pub and online.
think: I'll probably **waste half** the decade hoping it won't happen.
At **40** in 2039, with a worn body and no degree, starting over is hard.
do: Keep **working and saving** what little I can each month.
Look at a **substation course** in a few years, not straight away.
feel: **Unsettled**, less scared than with two years, but it **nags** on long drives.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds like a lot, but I know me, I'll waste half of it hoping it won't happen.
fieldNote: He's **honest about delay** and links it to how he handled his exams.
**Age 40** in 2039 is his biggest fear, more than the date itself.
Even with a decade, his first move is **politics**, not personal change.

steps.text: Keep working the valley crew and saving what he can
Campaign online and at the union for public ownership of the grid
Apply for a council flat to escape rising private rent

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, no question. What would help is the union having a deal ready before it lands, and the government paying for real retraining with a wage while you do it. I can't afford to study on nothing.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe how much this job is about trust. When the lights go out in a village, people come out with tea for us. A robot's never going to get a cup of tea from Mrs Evans at the farm on the hill.

headlineQuote: I can't afford to study on nothing.
portrait: Gareth is a **27-year-old** lineworker on a rural crew, living in a rented flat with his girlfriend Leila.
He has about **two weeks** of savings and depends on **storm overtime** to keep the household level.
He leans left, trusts the **union**, and blames bosses and government more than the technology.
He avoids new tech and **won't retrain** early, preferring to fight for a fair exit.
His mood runs from **uneasy** about rent in the calm picture to **alarmed** at AGI by 2028.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because robots would arrive while he's still young and unskilled elsewhere.
whatWouldHelp: A **union deal** agreed in advance and **paid retraining** with a wage while he studies.
